youtube.title: Python Mini Project: Word Counter | Python Programming EP 40
youtube.description: In this episode you will split text into words and count each one, make counting case-insensitive with lower() and print the results in order and find the most common word, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Planning the word counter · 0:51 The word counter · 1:31 Words and their counts · 2:03 Second program · 3:03 Recap · 3:37 Bug of the Day · 4:25 Challenge · 4:45 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Time for a project that puts the whole module together. Today we build a word counter.

scenes.onScreen: "Planning the word counter": three numbered lines (1. Read a line of text and make it lowercase; 2. Split it into words and count each; 3. Print the counts in order and the most common word) and an analogy card: a library assistant: read a page, tally every word, and report the favourite
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Here is the plan. Read a line of text. Make it lowercase, so The and the count as one word. Split it into words. Count each word in a dictionary. Then print the counts in alphabetical order, and name the most common word. It uses strings, lists, dictionaries and loops. And one new trick, max with a key, to find the biggest count.

scenes.onScreen: wordcount.py: count the words of a typed line
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right; faint indent guide lines
scenes.narration: [HL 1] Ask for a line of text. [HL 2] Make it lowercase, then split it into words. Chaining methods like this is common. [HL 3] An empty dictionary for the counts. [HL 4] Loop over the words. [HL 5] The counting pattern, with get. [HL 6] Loop over the sorted keys, so the output is alphabetical. [HL 7] Print each word and its count. [HL 8] Max over the dictionary finds the key with the biggest count. Key equals counts dot get, says, compare by the count.

scenes.onScreen: words tied to a list; counts tied to a dict from word to count
scenes.animation: Name tags pop in with their arrows to the objects (value and type shown, no addresses); when Python reads a name the arrow glows and the object lights up
scenes.narration: Here is the end state. Words is tied to a list of six lowercase words. Counts is tied to a dictionary with four keys, because the repeated words were merged. The word the has the count three. The list kept every word, and the dictionary kept the tallies. Two different shapes for two different questions.

scenes.onScreen: unique.py: how many words, and how many are unique
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A fixed sentence. [HL 2] Split into a list. [HL 3] The length of the list is every word, counting repeats. Six. [HL 4] Wrap the list in set, and the repeats vanish. The length is the number of unique words. Four. Sets and dictionaries are two different tools for similar questions.

code.source:
text = "the sea the sand the sun"
words = text.split()
print(len(words), "words")
print(len(set(words)), "unique")

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the command types with key-tick, output prints in mint with a ding

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One: Make the text lowercase before you split it. Two: split turns a sentence into a list of words. Three: counts dot get of word, 0 plus 1 tallies each word. Four: max of counts, key equals counts dot get finds the most common word. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: capital and small letters counted apart
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The word the appears twice, once with a capital T. Our dictionary treats them as two different words, each with a count of one. Strings are case sensitive. Call lower before split, and the two become one word, with a count of two.

shorts.title: The word counter plan
shorts.script: Let us build a word counter. Read a line of text. Make it lowercase, so capital letters do not matter. Split it into words. Count each word in a dictionary. Then print the counts in alphabetical order, and name the most common word. It uses strings, lists, dictionaries, and loops, so it is a perfect project to finish the module. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: A project for the whole module.

shorts.title: Lower, then split
shorts.hook: "The first two steps are one line."
shorts.script: The first two steps are one line. Text dot lower, dot split. Lower makes every letter small, so The and the become the same word. Split cuts the text at the spaces, and gives a list of words. Chaining methods like this is very common in Python. Read it left to right, one step at a time. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Chain the methods.

shorts.title: The most common word
shorts.hook: "To find the most common word, use max on the dictionary, with key equals counts dot get."
shorts.script: To find the most common word, use max on the dictionary, with key equals counts dot get. Normally, max compares the keys, the words, in alphabet order. The key option tells it to compare by the count instead. So you get the word with the biggest count. It is a very short answer to a very useful question. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: The winner of the count.

shorts.title: Case matters
shorts.script: Here is the quiet bug. The word the appears twice, once with a capital T. Your dictionary treats The and the as two different words, each with a count of one. There is no error, only a wrong answer. Strings are case sensitive. Call lower before you split, and the two become one word with a count of two. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Lower it first.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.hook: "Why did the word counter never get bored?"
shorts.script: Why did the word counter never get bored? It always had a lot to say. Your challenge. Run the word counter on a sentence of your own, with at least ten words. Then add a line that prints how many unique words there are. You can use the length of the dictionary. Share your sentence and your answer in the comments below. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 40.
